episodes.title: Episode 02: The teacher beats our best model
notes: Gated teacher (32 paired draws, gain > 2 SE and > 0.02): 56.2% vs c2 2654, 59.4% vs c1 2300 (160 games each, intervals above 50%)
It overrides about 4-5% of buys; ~1 s per buy
Student after 49.6k labels: dev regret 0.059 vs c2 0.047; dev score ~50%
Next: teacher confirmation on 200 reserved kingdoms vs c2 and c1
transcript: Last time, the teacher lost. It played our best model and won only about forty one percent of the games. It kept changing good buys on the strength of a lucky replay.

So I gave it one rule. It may only change the best model's buy when the gain is clear. The gain has to beat two standard errors of the measurement, and it has to be at least two points. Each choice now gets thirty two replays instead of sixteen.

With that rule the teacher changes only about one buy in twenty-five. And it wins. Against the newer version of our best model it scored fifty six percent over one hundred and sixty games. Against the older version it scored fifty nine percent. In both cases the uncertainty range stays above fifty percent. Those are the first numbers that beat the third reinforcement learning network.

Why does it work? The best model is very good, but it makes a few buys that it would regret if it could see the whole game play out. The teacher plays out each choice to the end, with the best model's own play afterwards, and keeps only the changes that clearly pay.
The catch is speed. The teacher needs about one second for each buy, because it plays a couple of hundred games in its head. For a game on Steam that is fine. For training and big tests it is slow.

That is why the small, fast network is still training. It has now seen about fifty thousand graded buys. It is learning, but slowly. Its picks still lose a little more value than the best model's own picks, so for now it almost never overrides. Its test games sit right at fifty percent. Each buy label is noisy, and it needs many more of them.

Next, a bigger check of the teacher runs on two hundred kingdoms it has never seen, against both versions of the best model. And the small network keeps collecting about twenty thousand graded buys an hour. If it starts to copy the teacher's few good changes, we get the same gain in one fast step.

episodes.title: Episode 01: A challenger that prices every buy
notes: Teacher: paired rollouts to the end of the game for c2's top 5 buys + PASS
Gate 1: teacher on c2 scored 41.5% after 100 games vs c2 (noise: winner's curse)
Student round 1 on 2,118 labels: flat outputs; fixed to rank only graded candidates and read c2's preferences
Training now: 20,000 labels per round, dev match of 600 games each round
Goal: >= 53% vs RL-v3 c1 2300 and c2 2654 on 2,000 reserved kingdoms
transcript: You asked for a new model that could beat our best one. So tonight I started a new project. It asks a simple question. What is each buy actually worth?

Our best model today is the third reinforcement learning network. It wins about eighty six percent of its games against the genetic algorithm base. It plays every decision with one network. When it buys a card, it says what it would buy. It never says how much better that card is than the next one.

The new project tries to measure exactly that. At each buy, a teacher takes the best model's top five choices, plus buying nothing. It plays each one to the very end of the game. Every choice sees the same shuffles of the hidden cards, so the comparison is fair. After that, the best model plays every move for both sides. The share of games won is the price of that buy.

The teacher is slow. One game where it grades every buy takes about half a minute. So the plan is to teach a small, fast network to predict those prices. It looks at the cards in the kingdom as a set, and it scores every buy in one step.

Before any of that, I tested the teacher itself against the best model. It lost. After one hundred games it had about forty one percent. The reason is noise. With only sixteen to thirty two replays per choice, the teacher often thinks a card is better when it was just lucky. It changed the best model's choice on about one buy in five, and many of those changes were mistakes.

The small network has a second chance, because it learns from many positions at once. Luck in one position cancels out across thousands of them. The first small network was trained on only two thousand positions. It learned nothing useful yet. Its prices were flat, and it picked cards it had never been shown. I fixed two things. It now only chooses among the cards the teacher actually graded. And it gets to see the best model's own preferences, so it starts close to them.

Training is running now. It collects twenty thousand graded buys per round, which takes about an hour on this laptop. After each round it plays six hundred test games against the best model. It only overrides a buy when it is confident by a margin.

What I expect is honest uncertainty. Buys differ by a few percent of win chance, and each label is far noisier than that. We probably need a hundred thousand positions or more before the network can see the signal. The goal is fifty three percent against both versions of the best model, on two thousand kingdoms it has never seen. If the dev games stay below fifty percent after a few rounds, I will say so, and we will look at why.
You can follow every round on the project site.
